correctness.rationale: Every circular run of least period p begins with a primitive p-square whose preceding letter prevents left extension. The primitive-square minimum-period claim follows from Fine-Wilf, the de Bruijn short-factor count is exact, and left/right boundary counts prove the general total and length formulas. A repeated n-window forbids p>=n and bounds the length by n+p-1. For binary order five, the exhaustive bijection of cycles with single-orbit 16-bit feedback tables gives a complete 65,536-case proof; independently generated Euler circuits give the same 2,048 cycles, and distinct maximal-equality and direct-interval detectors agree on every run. The actual standalone checker returned VERIFY_OK and asserts all six profile and period-length totals. No infinite statement is inferred from finite sampling.

originality.rationale: The main distinguishing contribution is the complete binary order-five circular maximal-run period profile, including the six exact multiplicities. The general low-period count is acknowledged as a fairly direct, though explicitly proved, consequence of uniform de Bruijn factor frequencies and primitive-square detection. Published global runs bounds, de Bruijn generation algorithms, and repetition-compression complexity bounds do not imply the cycle-dependent period-three/four profile. Indexed semantic and literature searches did not disclose a covering profile; unresolved historical priority remains a stated risk.

Unindexed or privately circulated tables of exact order-five de Bruijn circular runs cannot be excluded by negative search results.
The period-three and period-four finite classification depends on executable exhaustive enumeration, not a separate closed-form symbolic count of its six multiplicities.

value.rationale: The object is the canonical family of universal cyclic strings, and maximal repetitions are a classical string-algorithm invariant. A natural exact question asks which run statistics are forced by short-factor balance and which begin to depend on the Euler cycle. The general q-ary period and exact-length laws identify a rigid range, and the complete first large binary order-five census classifies the genuinely variable period-three/four boundary into exactly six period profiles and three total-run levels. This is a nontrivial complete natural finite classification with a reusable baseline for studying higher orders and checking circular run enumerators, not an arbitrary slice or re-labeled historical table.
